title: API Authentication and Authorization
learning_outcomes: Explain the main security concern and trust boundary involved in API Authentication and Authorization.
Choose an appropriate defensive control for API Authentication and Authorization and state the assumptions under which it works.
Define a safe, reproducible verification step for API Authentication and Authorization, including a relevant negative or failure case.

content.intro: This lesson belongs to Module 15: API, GraphQL, WebSocket, and Webhook Security. It builds practical understanding of API Authentication and Authorization with the syllabus subtopics retained below.
content.why_it_matters: API Authentication and Authorization addresses how untrusted data or requests cross a boundary and may influence application behavior. The safe fix should address the root cause and remain testable. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: API Authentication and Authorization can be understood through this sequence: Identify caller → Resolve resource → Enforce server policy → Test allow + deny. Start with the application asset and trust boundary, state what secure behavior should occur, and identify the evidence that would prove or disprove it.

content_blocks.title: Connect the syllabus subtopics
content_blocks.text: The source curriculum groups this lesson around: 107.1 Session-based and token-based authentication; 107.2 Endpoint-level authorization; 107.3 Object-level authorization; 107.4 Field-level authorization; 107.5 Function-level access controls; 107.6 Consistent authorization across API versions. Treat these points as a checklist, not a list to memorize: explain the risk, identify the root cause, select a control, and define a test for that control.

items.title: Scope
items.text: Identify the asset, principal, input, state, or boundary affected. State whether the example is local, owned, or explicitly authorized.

items.title: Control
items.text: Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.

items.title: Failure behavior
items.text: Include an invalid, denied, expired, malformed, repeated, or otherwise relevant boundary case. Fail safely without exposing secrets.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Record expected versus actual behavior, a sanitized request or test result, the root cause, the chosen fix, and the regression test.

content_blocks.title: Safe reference example: API Authentication and Authorization
content_blocks.expected_output: The function returns True only for a matching owner or an administrator role, assuming the identity and record came from trusted server-side lookups.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Illustrative policy function; adapt roles and object model, authenticate the caller, and test denied as well as allowed paths.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Use a clean local test account and synthetic data. Reset the test fixture after recording the result; do not include credentials or private data in the course report.

content_blocks.title: Common mistake and recovery
content_blocks.text: Do not confuse an observation with proof or rely on a UI-only restriction. Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases. If evidence is ambiguous, reduce the test to one condition, inspect the application code/configuration, and repeat only within the permitted scope.

content_blocks.title: Execution and safety boundary
content_blocks.text: The current CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview, not a secure runner for arbitrary server code. This example is a static reference unless the run instructions explicitly identify a supported local environment. Use a private local lab or a test system with written authorization; do not test unrelated public systems.

content.task: For “API Authentication and Authorization”, write a short security note or test in a local/owned application. Identify the expected secure behavior, at least one relevant failure case, and the evidence needed to prove the control works.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the core rule for API Authentication and Authorization in your own words.
Name the trust boundary and the server-side control or policy that applies.
Specify a repeatable test for expected behavior and a relevant denied/failure path.
Use synthetic data and redact credentials, tokens, and personal information from evidence.
hints: Start by stating the asset, input, actor, or trust boundary and the expected secure behavior.
Change one condition at a time; record expected and actual outcomes with synthetic data.
Check the linked official reference for framework-specific settings and version-dependent behavior.
content.expected_output: A concise control explanation and a sanitized test record showing expected/actual behavior, one failure case, and a regression check.
recap: API Authentication and Authorization is a security boundary/control topic, not a standalone checklist item.
Apply least privilege and default-deny authorization on the server for each relevant action, object, and property, then test both allowed and denied cases.
Retest fixes and record sanitized evidence; use only authorized environments.
